ARTEX and Friends: Enter Agentic Offensi: Written by: Aurora Blum, David Mainor, Rohit Nambiar, Omar ElAhdan, Matthew McWhirt, Will Silverstone, Bhavesh Dhake, Chris Busse Introduction Recent intrusions in which threat actors have been observed weaponizing agentic frameworks to execute highly-automated intrusions has put a spotlight on evolving adversarial use of LLMs. In our September 2026 report , Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) noted that forward leaning adversaries were beginning to transition from basic prompting to agentic workflows and LLM-enabled automation. Since this publication, GTIG and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike and CAIRN in incident response engagements to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. This activity has been seen across the threat landscape, as noted in a recent Wiz report . The emergence of Artex and similar agentic offensive intrusion frameworks underscores a broader shift toward threat actor adoption of open source multi-agent offensive frameworks, as well as potentially custom agentic harnesses. This represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling intrusions exponentially. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Security teams, developers, and system administrators will need to fundamentally rethink defense strategies to counter scalable, autonomous software. We also provide defensive strategies from Mandiant Consulting. The defensive strategies suggested—control-plane isolation, short-lived credentials, least privilege, segmentation, and behavioral detection—are long-standing security best practices. Observations in the Wild We are seeing tools used by adversaries evolving towards autonomous agentic attacks. One way this is occurring is through suites of tools or frameworks designed for penetration testing (“pentesting”). These tools and frameworks orchestrate various agents using open source and frontier LLMs to automate various stages of intrusions. Historically, cyber espionage and financially motivated threat actors have taken advantage of pentesting or red-teaming platforms built for security professionals to exploit systems, such as Cobalt Strike or Metasploit. Today, adversaries are pivoting toward offensive frameworks powered by LLMs. While these frameworks have existed in the wild, they are now yielding success in intrusions in the wild, representing a critical evolution that increases both the speed and scale of intrusion activity. Since late August 2026, we have observed threat actors actively operating popular open-source multi-agent pentesting platforms like ARTEX, PentAGI, CAIRN and other potentially custom harnesses within Mandiant incident response engagements; use of these platforms has been further corroborated by our research telemetry. In these incidents , we have observed agentic activity conducting significant parts of the attack lifecycle (e.g., lateral movement, database exploitation, exfiltration preparation). Evidence of in the wild usage of these frameworks marks a critical inflection point for defenders, as agents now autonomously explore multiple attack paths, troubleshoot errors, and achieve objectives in seconds and minutes. Coupled with continual advancements in underlying LLM capabilities, the acceleration in attack velocity and scale signals a notable shift in the threat landscape that fundamentally alters traditional intrusion dynamics. ARTEX Framework ARTEX is an autonomous, multi-agent LLM-driven pentesting and offensive command-and-control (C2) platform written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console. The framework was originally developed by the user Autumn-27 and released on GitHub. Although the original repository was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO. ARTEX abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents. By leveraging APIs from frontier and open source models, the framework translates high-level tactical goals into actionable machine commands. GTIG has observed capabilities including automated Active Directory reconnaissance, privilege escalation, target cloud-infrastructure profiling (such as harvesting Azure storage keys), to the synthesis and deployment of custom webshells. Since late August 2026, ARTEX has been adopted by a diverse range of threat actors across the motivational spectrum, including both financially motivated extortion groups and suspected cyber espionage operators. For example, the Wiz Research team has been tracking a campaign associated with ARTEX, which GTIG tracks as UNC7228, that overlaps with activity tracked by Microsoft as the PRC-nexus actor STORM-0940 . The research has expanded Wiz’s understanding of this campaign beyond the October IT focused activity with activity now dating back to at least August 2026. Wiz identified the targeting, compromise, and data theft affecting multiple entities in the US and Europe across the enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor manufacturing and design, and telecommunications industry verticals. This actor has moved extremely quickly, typically moving from their first compromised account to deep system access in around four hours and in one case as rapidly as 15 minutes. They have also customized their tooling to take advantage of victim-specific setups and fallen back to open proxies if their initial infrastructure was blocked. Demonstrating broader adoption of ARTEX, GTIG and Mandiant observed multiple other threat actors using ARTEX for post-compromise reconnaissance, lateral movement, and privilege escalation in incident response investigations. This includes financially motivated threat actors who used the framework to facilitate data theft extortion, and additional suspected PRC-nexus clusters. Their operations collectively impacted organizations across government, technology, chemicals and materials, and manufacturing sectors in the US, alongside public reporting of ARTEX targeting the financial sector in Asia. In several cases, adversaries provided ARTEX with compromised credentials for the targeted organization, and instructed the framework to execute subsequent stages of the attack lifecycle. Analysis of these intrusions reveals key differences between activity conducted by the ARTEX framework and that of a human operator: Based on log files and timestamps, we identified bursts of activity that would be highly irregular for a human operator. While each of the intrusions exhibited extended pauses during operational phases, individual ARTEX execution sequences ran in compressed bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds. In at least one operation, we observed 27 events in 23 seconds of active burst time, performing rapid probing of AWS permissions across different security groups. While preparing potential exfiltration scripts, ARTEX was capable of successfully adapting to errors quoting “script too large” by trimming the script and relaunching it to successfully deploy a 17-snapshot instance in approximately 10 seconds. Compared to a competent human operator, ARTEX achieved code execution in a far more forensically noisy manner, relying on rapid, iterative trial-and-error. In one instance, supplied with valid credentials, ARTEX accessed an external-facing Linux Weaver OA web server to execute SQL commands via exposed API calls. Using legitimately-exposed application-specific API calls, ARTEX was able to achieve partial command-execution to conduct further reconnaissance despite hitting technical complexities. However, this process generated 240 log events and exhibited errors potentially caused by multiple sub-agents overwriting one another while pursuing the same objective. In an attempt to pivot from a database-execution context to a system-execution context, ARTEX used an application-specific SQL API, accessible to the supplied-user credential, to modify the MySQL instance to write log files with a .jsp extension to publicly accessible locations. The SQL-commands executed were likely intended to poison MySQL logs into writing web-accessible JSP webshells. Using the API, ARTEX ran SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '<path to webshell>’ followed by SET GLOBAL general_log = 1 ; subsequent SQL commands were written to the filepath defined in general_log_file . ARTEX then ran SQL SELECT statements in the form `SELECT '<% [webshell content] %>'` . Due to how the underlying Java web servlet handles JSP files, the Java code in the '<% %>' gets parsed and compiled into the process memory space, providing means of execution. Log activity shows multiple iterations of the above sequence, with ephemeral, somewhat-incremental file names ( cl1217.jsp, f1219a.jsp, z1219.jsp ) for each webshell candidate, each one executing a different command. Errors when trying to run the webshell (e.g. variable ‘t is already defined ’) caused the webshell to fail and likely had ARTEX refactor its approach, writing several unique webshells, each with a different goal, some correcting previous errors until the .jsp webshells executed cleanly and returned valid command output to ARTEX. In another case, during access-probing efforts, ARTEX generated files of various extension types with the filename artex-probe-* , where * carried five digit somewhat-incremental numbers. Based on our visibility, it’s difficult to comment on the exact significance of these numbers or how they increment. However, ARTEX was seen using similar incremental numeric markers within dropped file names, created account names, their passwords and within email subjects. Observed ARTEX Activity Mapped along the phases of a targeted attack lifecycle Phase of the attack lifecycle Observed ARTEX Capabilities & Tradecraft Initial Recon Automatically mapped the effective permissions of obtained Azure credentials (SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, and Storage Account keys) using sub-second capability checks, test blob writes/deletes, and ARM deployment validation dry-run sweeps. This activity included bursts of rapid activity, with ARTEX writing and immediately deleting a tiny test blob in ~330–400 ms and running an 8-second ARM deployments/validate dry-run sweep across 11 Azure resource types. Tested compromised IAM user permissions using DryRun flags and placeholder IDs to evaluate EC2 compute, EBS volume, and snapshot capabilities. Over a span of over 500 web requests, ARTEX probes various file names and extensions across various web directories, in a potential attempt to fuzz which URL endpoints the web-server would allow it to access based on HTTP response code ( 200 or 403 ). Establish Foothold Abused Kudu administrative APIs to execute arbitrary commands and stage custom Python, C#, and malicious PowerShell scripts. Established command and control (C2) and execution on the victim's internal Windows database server by using native curl to pull down dynamically generated PowerShell and batch scripts and post back command results across 491 rotating webhook.site URLs. Escalate Privileges Attempted to escalate privileges by launching cloud compute instances with potentially high-value IAM roles with the intention of fetching the role’s temporary credentials and thereby escalating privileges in doing so. These attempts however seemed to have failed due to invalid instance profile ARNs. Escalated privileges by running Kerberoasting scripts to harvest service tickets across compromised domains; using SQL injection to dump database credentials; and, following an offline cracking pause, executing DCSync scripts to steal the domain krbtgt key, cloud AD-sync credentials, and domain Controller machine hashes. Created accounts with is_admin=true within minutes, identifying and utilizing a writable admin flag. Internal Recon Performed reconnaissance across the internal network by running several iterative generated PowerShell enumeration scripts against a Domain Controller and federation server. The scripts validated domain usernames without pre-authentication, listed Group Managed Service Accounts, audited Active Directory Certificate Services templates (SmartcardUser, ClientAuth), mapped thousands of cross-forest security principals, and swept internal Exchange, PasswordState credential vault, and SSRF/SCM targets. Move Laterally Attempted Lateral Movement onto domain controllers using Pass-the-Ticket, WinRM, Kerberos relay, and Pass-the-Hash scripts, hitting local Windows service token privilege restrictions right before endpoint protection blocked execution and defenders severed access to the server. Maintain Presence Generated a new SSH key pair, allocated a dedicated public Elastic IP, attempted to create a custom security group but failed due to permission issues, and launched persistent t3.micro instances bound to existing security groups to establish an externally addressable jump host and internal foothold. Gained persistence through account takeover (e.g., resetting passwords for identified users), creating multiple accounts with plaintext passwords (which included ArtexProbe in the naming convention), and creating administrator accounts. Complete Mission Interrogating backend SQL databases (extracting ~400 KB of query results across ~20 queries) and performing mass blob reads. Deployed custom boot scripts via ephemeral, keyless EC2 instances to potentially harvest data from multiple mounted EBS snapshots and volumes. Enumerated over 110,000 Active Directory objects from a domain controller and retrieved the Domain Admins group. It then sent command output to rotating webhook.site endpoints via curl. Ran queries to decrypt stored notes and attempted to read other users' note attachments. Created a new 100GB volume and expanded the root disk of launched instances to 60GB, performing preparatory steps likely intended for exfiltration via their automated collection scripts. Edited an employee's record in a legacy database, created and deleted notes and status rows, pointed checklist responses at its own probe file. In this case we observed an interesting abuse of legitimate features. Rather than executing complex malware, ARTEX weaponized built-in application features. It forced an application's notification system to broadcast test emails to over 1,300 internal users, turning a trusted notification channel into a mass-internal messaging tool. It then dropped to single-recipient test emails rather than the mass emailing. PentAGI Offensive Framework GTIG also observed in the wild abuse of PentAGI (Penetration Testing Artificial General Intelligence), an autonomous offensive framework designed to automate the pentesting process within an isolated environment. Developed by VXControl, the framework is offered in an open source and commercial edition. It is designed so that the user only needs to describe a target and a goal, which enables entry-level users to run complex cyber security campaigns. Once the target and the goal have been selected, the framework uses a team of specialized agents, each with their own functionalities to break tasks (called “Flows”) into various sub-tasks, execute each step, and report on it. The tools and commands are all run in isolated sandboxes running Kali Linux instead of in the host environment. All the tools used by PentAGI are open-source pentesting tools available by default in Kali Linux (e.g., metasploit, nmap, SQLmap). The framework supports over a dozen cloud and local LLM backends, including frontier and open weight models. The majority of observed PentAGI activity remained at the stage of WHOIS asset mapping or active vulnerability scanning. However, analysis of operational artifacts indicates that some operations progressed to active intrusions and persistence across multiple organizations. Operators are also adapting and integrating the framework in different ways. In one case, we identified a customized attack orchestration platform built on the open-source version of PentAGI likely used between at least late August and early October 2026 to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia, including system integrators and major telecommunications firms. In another instance, we observed PentAGI chained with proxy services to target the Aerospace sector. Evolution of Autonomous Offensive Frameworks We are seeing a significant maturation in the application of LLM capabilities across the threat landscape in a short period of time; this includes the incorporation of LLM-written malicious code, development of dynamic LLM-enabled malware, poisoning of agent-harness files, and the building of multi-agent offensive frameworks. Notably, between late 2025 and October 2026, autonomous and semi-autonomous offensive frameworks crossed a decisive operational threshold to multi-agent frameworks actively weaponized by threat actors to perform in the wild intrusions. GTIG has been tracking the evolution of this experimentation over time, from simple prompting of LLMs to help with coding, through the use of frameworks in the wild towards a potential future with fully autonomous frameworks running intrusions. In a fully autonomous attack, a human’s role would consist of telling the agent what to target, and then simply benefiting from the operational objective. At the time of reporting, we assess that the current adversary use of autonomous offensive frameworks is still in early stages characterized by open source tools currently being used in low-sophisticated ways, resulting in broad and noisy, but still successful campaigns. As the sophistication of these frameworks, the underlying LLMs and the orchestrating human-operator increase, we expect to see not only less human interaction, but also increased stealth and sophistication. The following stages represent our observations of how LLM-augmentation in cyber operations have evolved over the last year and how we expect this development to continue: Stage 1: Prompt-based use of LLMs Activity : Adversaries interact with LLMs in a prompt based chatbot fashion, using LLMs to write and debug code for malware, draft phishing emails, create personas, and conduct light reconnaissance on targets. Evolution : Adversaries outsource low-failure, easy-to-rectify, tasks to an LLM to increase speed of simple discrete tasks. Timeframe: End of 2025 to early 2026 Stage 2: Embedding LLM capabilities into malware Activity : Adversaries trust an LLM to take certain low-failure, easy to execute actions, particularly writing code, such as in malware families like HONESTCUE or PROMPTSPY using LLMs dynamically during execution to, for example, obfuscate payloads in different ways in attempts to evade defenses. Evolution : Adversaries begin use incorporating LLMs into post-intrusion attack phases. Timeframe : Early 2026 Stage 3: Incorporating LLM-enabled automation into operations Activity : As agentic capabilities develop, adversaries begin using them for discrete tasks (e.g., standing up or debugging malware development environments). Agents begin being used alongside human-operators to develop novel exploits and to assist with high-stake vulnerability research. Adversaries begin being more cognizant of OPSEC and visibility into their LLM-usage operations and start using LLM-proxy services to obscure activities. Evolution : LLMs being used for more high-stake tasks but with human operators in the loop. Timeframe : Early 2026 - September 2026 Stage 4: Developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks Activity : Adversaries begin developing and experimenting with autonomous frameworks. Campaigns begin offloading more stages of the lifecycle to LLM-augmented tooling, and integrating model APIs into their tools and telegram bots to take autonomous action. Evolution : Experimentation with LLMs running more stages of the attack lifecycle. Timeframe : Mid 2026 - September 2026 Stage 5: Multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling in the wild Activity : In the wild evidence of multiple attack lifecycle stages being conducted by LLM-driven tooling, with fewer humans in the loop during operations. Observations surrounding mass-exploitation campaigns where a substantial portion of the lifecycle is being carried out by an agent, requiring only minimal human intervention, as well as activity accompanied by malware possessing more autonomous capabilities. Additionally, continued experimentation by threat actors with better obfuscation—including LLM mixers, inference services, local models. Overall TTPs of these attacks remain messy, noisy but yet successful. Evolution : Adversaries have actively integrated LLMs into their operations to conduct successful intrusions, while simultaneously exploring ways to obscure/reduce reliance on frontier-lab LLMs. Timeframe : Current stage of development Stage 6: Multi-agent-driven, unsophisticated attacks with little to no human interaction Activity : Highly-autonomous, but unsophisticated, forensically noisy operations with human operators no longer in the loop. Adversaries define the target and objective, while multi-agent frameworks execute the entire attack chain and return operational objectives. Evolution : Adversaries diversifying infrastructure and tooling, further inhibiting defenders’ visibility. Timeframe : Near-term (1 - 3 months) Stage 7:  Sophisticated, fully autonomous/agentic attacks Activity : This stage represents peak maturity on the offensive LLMs capability curve, characterized not only by fully autonomous intrusions requiring little to no human interaction, but also by increased stealth and sophistication of the activity, with operators interacting with LLMs through either obscurely designed infrastructure or self-hosted LLMs altogether. Evolution : This stage would grant autonomous and stealthier operations while limiting defender’s visibility into the activity. Timeframe : Medium-term (3 - 6 months) We believe malicious actors will continue to experiment with these offensive agentic frameworks, moving towards future autonomous usage. GTIG has observed evidence of threat-actor experimentation with tools like the ZeroHollow inference service and the fully agentic framework AgentZero . Outlook Over the past 12 months, GTIG has observed a decisive evolution in adversarial tradecraft leveraging LLMs, progressing from ad hoc operational productivity support toward the deployment of coordinated, multi-agent, autonomous offensive frameworks. While earlier milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted early agentic interest, recent observations across frontline incident response engagements and proactive intelligence collection reveals adversary adoption of these frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during intrusions. Threat actors are increasingly leveraging generative models to achieve unprecedented speed and scale, actively developing more complex attack infrastructure powered by agentic AI capabilities and AI-enabled automation. Frameworks such as ARTEX compress attack timelines to machine speed; however, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces, increasing the likelihood of detection and mitigation. These tools are therefore best suited to scenarios in which the cost of detection is low. Additionally, detection and disruption/response are two different functions–simply detecting the attack in time does little to hinder objective completion. Consequently, GTIG assesses with high confidence that cyber crime threat actors will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates. We anticipate that actors, who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term access, are less likely to use the publicly available versions of these tools, though they may employ them for purposes of scale and speed, depending on operational priorities. Regardless of motivation, the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential make autonomous frameworks an attractive, low-cost force multiplier for a wide range of threat actors, making it highly likely that we will continue to see increasing threat actor adoption of these types of frameworks in the near term. Defending Against AI-Enabled Attacks: Five Layers of Defense LLM-enabled offensive tooling does not fundamentally change the techniques attackers use. It reduces the time required to combine them. Credential discovery, permission testing, lateral movement, and data access that previously required hours of operator effort can now occur in minutes, frequently through valid identities and supported functionality that static indicators will not detect. Organizations are best positioned to withstand this when compromise of a single identity, credential, or workload provides only limited access. Restricting control-plane exposure, replacing long-lived secrets with short-lived and tightly scoped credentials, segmenting application tiers, and placing guardrails on high-impact business functions all reduce the speed advantage automation provides. Behavioral detection addresses the activity that these controls do not prevent, but it depends on having sufficient identity, control-plane, data-plane, and network telemetry to establish what normal activity looks like. Many of these controls are already familiar to defenders. The difference is that automated tooling can now identify and exploit the gaps between them far more quickly. As illustrated above, LLM-enabled offensive tooling is increasing the speed and scale of cyber attacks. LLM-enabled and autonomous tools can identify weaknesses, test access, interpret errors, adjust their approach, and continue through an attack path with limited human interaction. Work that might previously have required an operator to investigate an environment, write or modify code, troubleshoot failures, and execute the next step over several hours can increasingly happen in minutes. This creates a detection challenge as well. Much of the activity may use valid credentials and supported functionality (living-off-the-land, LotL). An attacker may authenticate with a legitimate service principal, call a normal management API, access cloud storage through a supported protocol, or execute commands through an existing administrative interface. Tool names, hashes, IP addresses, and other static indicators provide useful signals when available, but they will not cover much of this activity. Effective defenses combine two capabilities: Controls that limit what an attacker can do after gaining valid access. Telemetry that shows when an identity, application, or workload begins operating outside its normal pattern. How Adversarial Use of LLMs Changes the Attacker Timeline Several themes repeatedly appear during investigations involving LLM-enabled or highly automated attacker activity: Speed and scale : Automated tooling can perform broad reconnaissance, test several attack paths at once, react to failures, and immediately continue into follow-on activity. The time between initial access, privilege discovery, lateral movement, and data access can become very short. Interconnected environments : Attackers rarely remain inside one technology stack. An internet-facing application may expose credentials in a configuration file. Those credentials may provide access to cloud storage, source repositories, identity systems, or internal infrastructure. Automation makes it easier to discover and test those relationships quickly. Legitimate-looking identity activity : Many actions look normal when viewed independently. A service principal authenticates, an API is called, a storage object is downloaded. The stronger signal often comes from context: where the request originated, how much activity occurred, what happened immediately before and after it, and whether the behavior is expected for that identity. Control-plane and data-plane blind spots : Many organizations have mature endpoint monitoring but considerably less visibility into management APIs, programmatic identities, and cloud storage activity. Permission testing, retrieval of storage keys, bulk downloads, firewall changes, and management API calls may all be logged without generating useful alerts. Mandiant recommends structuring enterprise defenses across five foundational layers designed to restrict lateral movement and limit the speed advantage of autonomous tooling: Layer Description Layer 1: Protect Control Planes Restrict all admin APIs, consoles & CI/CD to trusted networks Layer 2: Restrict Identities & Keys Migrate to short-lived workload credentials; eliminate secrets Layer 3: Harden Configurations Continuous vulnerability scanning across apps & infrastructure Layer 4: Application Protections Harden applications to prevent abuse of legitimate features and capabilities Layer 5: Detect Behavioral Changes Monitor identity velocity, API bursts, and volumetric anomalies Table 1: Foundational layers for restricting adversarial LLM speed advantage and lateral movement Layer 1: Protect the Control Plane Restrict access to the systems attackers can use to administer, deploy, or reconfigure the environment. The control plane extends well beyond Active Directory or a cloud console. It includes identity providers, cloud management APIs, network and firewall management platforms, virtualization infrastructure, code repositories, CI/CD systems, privileged access management platforms, backup infrastructure, certificate authorities, SaaS administration consoles, and application administration interfaces. Why It Is Important Internet-accessible management interfaces can quickly become part of an attack path after credentials are obtained. For example, Azure App Service includes an administrative interface through Kudu Site Control Manager, or SCM, which supports application deployment and management functionality. If an attacker obtains publishing credentials or another identity capable of accessing that interface, automation can quickly test authentication, enumerate functionality, interact with application files, execute commands, retrieve output, and remove staged artifacts. Similar exposure exists across firewall administration, virtualization consoles, cloud management APIs, backup platforms, CI/CD interfaces, and other management services. Any reachable administrative path gives an automated attacker another capability to test. Mitigations Reduce Administrative Internet Exposure : Restrict cloud administration, network device management, application publishing interfaces, hypervisors, backup platforms, and other sensitive services to trusted networks, private connectivity, or dedicated administrative paths wherever possible. Require Trusted Administrative Paths : Require privileged users to administer sensitive infrastructure from managed devices, privileged access workstations, or approved jump hosts. Pair these controls with phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2 or passkeys where supported. Harden Application Management Interfaces : Treat application administration and publishing endpoints as privileged infrastructure rather than extensions of the public application. Configure access restrictions for Kudu/SCM endpoints separately where appropriate. Limit SCM access to approved management networks or deployment infrastructure. Disable basic publishing authentication where it is not required. Restrict access to deployment and publishing credentials. Consider deployment models such as run-from-package that reduce direct modification of deployed application files. Control Public Exposure by Design : Establish governance around public IP allocation and require architecture review before workloads or management interfaces are exposed directly to the internet. Apply Similar Controls to Programmatic Administration : Where supported, restrict administrative service principals and automation identities to expected networks, workloads, or private connectivity. Monitor the Control Plane as a Distinct Security Surface : Centralize authentication, configuration change, deployment, and administrative telemetry from cloud platforms, application administration interfaces, network infrastructure, backup platforms, and other management systems. Alert on administrative access from previously unseen networks, hosting providers, or geographies. Layer 2: Restrict Identities and Keys Reduce the value of stolen credentials by limiting their lifetime, permissions, and where they can be used. Security programs have traditionally placed more emphasis on human identities. Service principals, service accounts, API keys, storage keys, cloud access keys, deployment tokens, personal access tokens, and application secrets can receive less scrutiny despite providing significant access. Programmatic identities are especially useful to an automated attacker when they combine long-lived credentials, broad permissions, limited conditional controls, and limited monitoring. Why It Is Important Consider an exposed cloud storage credential. Once automated tooling discovers the credential in source code, an environment variable, application configuration, a database, or another compromised system, it can immediately test the credential and begin enumerating available data. A long-lived credential that works from anywhere on the internet and provides broad storage access can turn a single credential exposure into large-scale data access very quickly. The same pattern applies to service principals and other programmatic identities. A credential intended for an internal CI/CD runner carries considerably more risk when the identity can also authenticate from an arbitrary network  and access production resources. Credential security therefore needs to address both what an identity can access and the conditions under which that access is valid. Mitigations Prioritize Workload and Programmatic Identities : Apply the same rigor used for privileged human identities to service principals, service accounts, API keys, cloud access keys, application credentials, deployment tokens, and Personal Access Tokens. These identities should have defined owners, lifecycle controls, least privilege, monitoring, and incident response procedures. Move From Long-Lived to Short-Lived Credentials : Remove persistent secrets and use temporary or workload-bound credentials wherever possible. Transition from static AWS IAM access keys to temporary credentials through IAM roles. Replace Azure Service Principal client secrets with Managed Identities. Disallow Azure Storage Account Shared Key Authentication in favor of Entra ID authorization with Conditional Access Policies. Use Google Cloud Workload Identity Federation instead of long-lived service-account keys. Move from GitHub classic PATs to fine-grained PATs or workload-based authentication such as GitHub Actions OIDC where supported. Constrain Both the Where and the What : Limit non-human identities to the APIs, subscriptions, projects, repositories, storage resources, and systems that they actually require. Where supported, restrict the locations and workloads from which those identities can authenticate. A service principal used by an internal CI/CD runner should not also be usable from arbitrary external infrastructure. Hardening multi-cloud service principals requires replacing long-lived, static credentials with short-lived tokens and strictly enforcing access controls. Essential approaches across major providers include: Google Cloud : Using Workload Identity Federation and targeted IAM constraints. AWS : Leveraging OIDC federation combined with Service Control Policies (SCPs). Azure : Applying Conditional Access policies to restrict access contextually. Okta : Implementing Private Key JWT authentication along with network-restricted Authentication Policies. Use private connectivity, expected source ranges, workload federation, resource policies, and IAM conditions where appropriate across cloud platforms. Restrict AWS IAM Role Delegation : Tightly control permissions that allow one identity to assign or pass another identity’s privileges. In AWS, restrict iam:PassRole to specific roles and intended services and apply conditions such as iam:PassedToService where appropriate. Isolate Credential and Secret Stores : Place enterprise password vaults and secret management systems behind tightly controlled administrative and network paths. Require strong authentication for privileged access, restrict programmatic access to expected workloads and networks where supported, and alert on unusual bulk secret queries, enumeration, or export activity. These detections overlap with legitimate automation; the signal is in the identity, origin, volume, and sequence, not the action. Baseline known-good automation first and alert on deviation, or expect false positives on routine activity. Harden Password Reset and Account Lifecycle Processes : Require strong re-authentication or additional identity verification for high-risk password resets and account recovery. Monitor unusual bursts of password resets, account creation, credential additions, permission changes, or other lifecycle activity. Automate Secret Hygiene : Implement continuous scanning of repositories, container images, build artifacts, and pipelines for exposed secrets and credentials. Remove credentials from application code, configuration files, deployment scripts, and databases and move them into dedicated secret-management platforms. Rotate exposed credentials promptly rather than relying on removal from source-control history. Layer 3: Harden Configurations and Reduce Attack Paths Remove weaknesses that provide an initial foothold and limit how far a compromised workload can reach. Automated tooling is particularly effective in environments where several smaller weaknesses can be combined into a larger attack path. An exposed application, an overly privileged workload identity, a credential in an environment variable, and unrestricted network access may each appear manageable in isolation. Together, they can provide a direct path into sensitive systems. Why It Is Important A vulnerability in an internet-facing application may initially appear isolated. In practice, that application may have access to a backend database. The database may contain credentials. Application environment variables may contain cloud tokens. The underlying host may have an attached cloud identity with access to storage, secrets, or management APIs. Automation can test those paths in rapid succession. Failures can also become useful feedback. An application error, stack trace, database response, compiler output, or API error may give the tooling enough information to modify its next request within seconds. Detailed diagnostic information exposed externally therefore provides more than troubleshooting value; it can accelerate experimentation during an attack. Mitigations Continuously Reduce the External Attack Surface : Scan internet-facing applications and infrastructure for vulnerabilities, exposed administrative services, default configurations, and unnecessary services. Vulnerability programs should include custom applications, frameworks, libraries, and dependencies in addition to operating systems. Assume the Workload Can Be Compromised : Design applications so compromise of the front end provides access only to the systems required for that application’s function. Reduce application permissions and limit access to required databases, APIs, queues, storage accounts, and backend services. Enforce Application-Tier Segmentation : Segment internet-facing applications from identity infrastructure, management systems, and unrelated internal services. Restrict DMZ workloads from initiating unnecessary Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP, SMB, RDP, SSH, database, and administrative connections into internal networks. Harden Database Runtime Privileges : Application database accounts should not have broad administrative privileges. Restrict capabilities that allow a database engine or application identity to execute operating-system commands, write arbitrary files, modify server-wide settings, or cross the database-to-OS boundary unless the application requires them. Reduce Credential Exposure in Workloads : Review application configurations, environment variables, infrastructure-as-code, deployment scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and databases for embedded secrets. Compromise of one workload should not expose credentials for unrelated systems. Limit Error Feedback to External Users : Avoid returning detailed stack traces, compiler messages, SQL errors, internal paths, framework details, or other diagnostic information to unauthenticated users. Keep detailed troubleshooting information in internal logs. Harden Network and Security Appliances : Remove unnecessary management services from routers, firewalls, VPN appliances, and other infrastructure. Review configurations for unexpected accounts, scheduled jobs, startup scripts, configuration changes, and persistence mechanisms. Validate firmware integrity and vendor signatures where supported. Harden Active Directory Certificate Services : Review AD CS for certificate templates and enrollment paths that could allow an attacker to obtain authentication certificates or escalate privileges. Remove ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT where it is not required, particularly on templates supporting client authentication. Restrict enrollment permissions to the identities that require them. Require certificate manager or CA approval for higher-risk enrollment scenarios where appropriate. Enable Extended Protection for Authentication on applicable CA web interfaces where supported. Monitor unusual certificate enrollment involving privileged users or unexpected requesting systems. Reduce Credential Replay and Relay Opportunities : Enable Windows Credential Guard where appropriate, use Protected Users for suitable privileged accounts, enforce SMB signing, and enforce LDAP signing and channel binding. Reduce or disable NTLM where operationally feasible and continue hardening against credential relay, Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket, and related techniques. Restrict Unnecessary Authentication From Exposed Workloads : Internet-facing servers should only initiate Kerberos, NTLM, LDAP, SMB, WinRM, or RDP traffic to systems where those protocols are explicitly required. Layer 4: Harden Application Development Harden legitimate enterprise functionality that attackers can reuse after gaining access. A large portion of attacker activity relies on capabilities already present in the environment. Applications, authentication protocols, administrative services, scripting environments, messaging systems, deployment platforms, and business workflows may provide everything needed to continue an intrusion without introducing new malware. Automation makes these capabilities easier to discover and use quickly. Why It Is Important Internal business applications, scripts, and APIs are often customized to each organization without public documentation, and require a level of insider knowledge to understand exploitation opportunities. Automated LLM-powered offensive tooling has enabled attackers to enumerate and rapidly understand these internal applications and use them to their advantage. Internal communication functionality is one example. A compromised application account may legitimately have access to a notification, messaging, or email API. Sending messages is expected behavior for that application. That same capability can be abused to send hundreds or thousands of phishing messages. Without recipient limits, rate limits, or behavioral monitoring, a standard business function can become a high-speed distribution mechanism. Mitigations Put Guardrails Around High-Impact Business APIs : Applications capable of accessing sensitive data, retrieving credentials, sending email, notifications, creating users, modifying access, or performing other high-impact actions should have rate limits, recipient limits, transaction thresholds, and abuse controls appropriate to their function. Alert when an application operates materially outside its normal volume. Inventory Legitimate Administrative Capabilities Before an Incident: Security teams should know which platforms provide remote command execution, deployment, scripting, certificate issuance, identity synchronization, bulk messaging, and other high-impact functions. Those capabilities should have appropriate restrictions and monitoring in place before they are used during an intrusion. Conduct Automated Application Testing and Threat Modelling : All internal applications should have SAST and DAST scans conducted and findings resolved prior to deployment. Organizations can also leverage LLM-enabled tooling to automate the discovery, triage, reproduction, and patching of software vulnerabilities and potential attack paths. Organizations can also apply agentic source-code review and continuous AI-assisted vulnerability testing—whether a bespoke LLM harness or a managed capability such as Google AI Threat Defense —to find, triage, and reproduce these attack paths before an attacker does. Layer 5: Detect Behavioral and Volumetric Change Detect when identities, applications, workloads, and infrastructure begin operating outside their established patterns. Many actions performed during an automated attack are legitimate operations when viewed individually. Detection therefore depends heavily on context: identity, source network, volume, timing, sequence, target resource, and historical activity. Why It Is Important A service principal accessing cloud storage is not necessarily suspicious. A service principal that normally accesses ten objects from one internal network and suddenly downloads thousands of objects from an unfamiliar hosting provider is a different situation. Outbound activity provides similar context. Automated tooling on a compromised server may contact external webhook services to confirm execution or transfer results. It may also communicate with LLM platforms, temporary file-sharing infrastructure, tunneling services, or attacker-controlled systems. A single HTTPS connection may be routine. A production server that historically communicates with a small set of known destinations and suddenly begins reaching several new external services deserves closer attention. Mitigations and Detection Priorities Baseline Behavior at the Identity and Workload Level : Establish expected authentication sources, APIs, resources, activity volumes, and communication patterns for sensitive service principals, applications, workloads, and administrative identities. Detect Changes in Authentication Origin : Track the networks, ASNs, cloud regions, hosting providers, and other infrastructure used by privileged users and workload identities. Investigate successful authentication from infrastructure that falls outside the identity’s normal pattern. Monitor Control-Plane Velocity : Alert on unusual bursts of management API calls, permission testing, configuration changes, resource enumeration, credential retrieval, and other administrative activity. The timing and sequence of legitimate API calls can provide important context. Baseline Data-Plane Activity : Establish normal read, write, and object-access patterns for sensitive storage and data platforms. Detect sudden enumeration, unusual write-read-delete sequences, large increases in object access, or material changes in bytes transferred. Build Detections Around Sequences : Correlate related events across identity, control-plane, data-plane, endpoint, and network telemetry. A new authentication source followed by permission probing, storage enumeration, bulk downloads, and a connection to a previously unseen external service should be analyzed as one sequence. Monitor East-West Behavior From Exposed Workloads : Detect unexpected LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM, SMB, database, remote administration, and port-scanning activity originating from DMZ or internet-facing systems. Control and Monitor Server Egress : Restrict unnecessary outbound internet connectivity from production servers and route sensitive workloads through controlled egress paths where practical. Monitor previously unseen destinations, particularly webhook services, OAST infrastructure, tunneling platforms, public file-transfer services, and external AI platforms that are not required by the workload. Preserve the Telemetry Needed to See the Behavior : Collect and centralize interactive and non-interactive identity logs, service-principal authentication, cloud control-plane activity, sensitive storage data-plane logs, application administration logs, network flow, DNS, proxy telemetry, and endpoint activity. Establishing normal behavior depends on having enough historical data to compare against current activity. Google Security Operations (SecOps) Google SecOps customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Mandiant Frontline Threats and Mandiant Hunting Rules rule pack. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names: Suspicious Webhook.Site Interaction Suspicious Curl Invocation Cmd Launching Curl AWS Cloud Accounts Getcalleridentity Posted in Threat Intelligence
ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust:
Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram Introduction On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files. During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221 ), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders. Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public. Exploitation Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog . Post-Exploitation Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection. Figure 1: ARMORY CASTLE BeyondTrust compromise sequence of events Staging Webshell After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp . Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/ . ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion. SAWFLY Webshell SAWFLY ( mangoapi.php ) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe . If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found ( http_response_code(404) ) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval() . Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client. Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable ( /bin/sh ) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd . The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system. After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset. Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault: /ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile. Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials. The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored i n /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files. /usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;' Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs Persistence For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account. First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist . The contents of the zz-root-persist script indicate that it first checks if the user account is already granted passwordless root privileges within the /ns/config/sudoers.template file. If the entry is missing, the script appends '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to the template. This entry added  to the sudoers template grants the site user account passwordless administrative privileges to execute any command on the host system. Finally, the script executes '/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc , which forces the appliance backend to immediately parse /ns/config/sudoers.template and rebuild the active /etc/sudoers file. This strategy ensures the threat actor's privilege escalation survives system reboots and configuration resets, which would normally overwrite manual changes made directly to /etc/sudoers . #!/bin/bash
grep -qF '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' '/ns/config/sudoers.template' || echo '%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' >> '/ns/config/sudoers.template'
'/ns/sbin/bt-sysconfig' --no-restart misc Figure 4: Contents of zz-root-persist Anti-Forensics Throughout their unauthorized access to the appliance, Mandiant observed multiple instances where the threat actor attempted to impair defenses and hinder detection by systematically deleting system, web server, and application-level logs. Originating from the SAWFLY webshell, the threat actor executed the following command using elevated sudo privileges to delete active logs across both host and site-specific directories: 'rm -f \'/ns/log/auth.log\' \'/ns/log/ssl.log\' \'/ns/log/proto-handler.log\' \'/ns/log/bt-docker.log\' \'/ns/log/http-access.log\' \'/ns/log/http-errors.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm.log\' \'/ns/log/php-fpm-access.log\' \'/ns/log/php_debug.log\' \'/ns/log/php_web_errors.log\' \'/var/log/messages\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log\' \'/home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_error.log\' /tmp/sshauth.*' Figure 5: Recovered Command Lateral Movement: BeyondTrust Admin Session Abuse After the compromise of the BeyondTrust device, the threat actor pivoted into the BeyondTrust Remote Support application to perform reconnaissance via compromised Administrator credentials. First, the threat actor leveraged the Administrator account to log into the web administrative portal. {
  "event": "login",
  "status": "success",
  "target": "web/login",
  "who": "[REDACTED_USERNAME] using password",
  "who_ip": "[REDACTED_IP]"
} Figure 6: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry After testing their initial access and verifying their ability to temporarily join the native Administrators group policy, the threat actor altered their strategy for long-term persistence. The actor directly modified the compromised account's permissions, upgrading both local Jump Items and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator . Jump Items are individual systems or devices that are made available for remote access within a Jump Group, enabling administrators to organize and control access to remote systems. This configuration change granted the threat actor permanent, unrestricted authorization to launch remote sessions to downstream systems populated within the appliance's Jump Item list. {
  "event": "user_changed",
  "old_username": "[REDACTED]",
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 1,
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:id": 3,
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "No Access",
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:default:name": "Administrator",
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 1,
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:id": 3,
  "old_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "No Access",
  "new_permissions:jump_item_role:teams:name": "Administrator"
} Figure 7: BeyondTrust Syslog Entry Internal Reconnaissance Once the threat actor obtained elevated administrative privileges, Mandiant observed the threat actor establish a remote support session to target internal endpoints. Once connected, the threat actor leveraged the appliance’s built-in support tools to request and obtain full file-system access. The threat actor utilized the native BeyondTrust Remote Support file transfer service to download and exfiltrate sensitive internal documents useful for network reconnaissance, such as software inventories, directly from the user's desktop environment. BARECLAW Tunneler Mandiant observed the threat actor tunnel traffic through the BeyondTrust device via a custom SOCKS5 proxy tunneler. BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that provides a SOCKS5 proxy service carried over the WebSocket transport and relays TCP connections between a remote client and destinations. BARECLAW statically embeds a CivetWeb WebServer to supply its HTTP and WebSocket functionality and utilizes OpenSSL for TLS. BARECLAW is configurable and provides the option to require authentication, to encrypt data between the client and tunneler, to restrict reachable destinations to specific CIDR ranges, to chain traffic to an upstream proxy, and to modify its default WebSocket endpoint and listening ports. TLS is enabled by providing a PEM certificate while authentication, encryption, destination filtering, and TLS are disabled by default. BARECLAW receives its configuration through CLI input and it provides a CLI option menu: Usage: %s [options]
  --listen PORT            plain ws port (default 8080)
  --listen-tls PORT        wss port (default 8443, needs --ssl-cert)
  --ssl-cert FILE          PEM certificate (enables wss)
  --token STRING           shared secret (?token= auth + obfs seed)
  --obfs                   enable XOR stream obfuscation
  --timeout SEC            idle timeout (default 300)
  --connect-timeout SEC    target connect timeout (default 10)
  --max-tunnels N          concurrent tunnel limit (default 100)
  --allow-net CIDR         allowed target subnet (repeatable)
  --upstream [socks5://]host:port   route via upstream SOCKS5
  --threads N              civetweb worker threads (default 64)
  --ws-path PATH           websocket endpoint path (default /wsproxy)
  -q, --quiet              zero output (all logging suppressed)
  -h                       this help Figure 8: BARECLAW CLI Option Menu The threat actor executed BARECLAW through the following command line arguments: /tmp/ingredi_ws --listen 19800 --token %REDACTED% --obfs -q --ws-path /uidchanarge Figure 9: BARECLAW full Command-Line Arguments This command line configures BARECLAW to listen on TCP port 19800 and create the WebSocket endpoint /uidchanarge on the victim system. Clients are required to authenticate using the token specified in the command line arguments while the -q argument suppresses the tunneler’s logging. Tunneled data is encrypted with an XOR-based routine derived from that token and an 8-byte value provided by the client at the start of the session. The lack of the --ssl-cert and --listen-tls arguments in the CLI options means TLS was not enabled in this specific instance. Modifications to Haproxy.conf In addition to the creation of the BARECLAW tunneler, Mandiant observed the threat actor modify the /ns/config/haproxy.conf file in order for BARECLAW to be accessible directly from the internet. The HAProxy service running on BeyondTrust devices acts a reverse proxy for the device that accepts incoming requests on behalf of the BeyondTrust server and forwards the request to the appropriate backend services running on the local system (such as web interfaces, administration portals, or application gateways) based on the request's port or URL path. The haproxy.conf file is the primary configuration script that dictates how the BeyondTrust appliance handles, routes, and secures incoming traffic. The threat actor modifications first established an Access Control List (ACL) named wswsws to monitor incoming traffic for the specific URI path /uidchanarge . When a request matching this path is detected, HAProxy bypasses normal appliance web services and routes the traffic to a custom backend designated as webskd3 . acl wswsws path /uidchanarge
    use_backend webskd3 if wswsws Figure 10: ACL Modification to haproxy.conf Next, the webskd3 backend routes the incoming web stream locally (127.0.0.1 / localhost) to TCP port 19800, where the BARECLAW utility is actively listening. This local-only binding ensures that the backdoor listener remains completely hidden from external network scans, as it can only be reached internally via HAProxy's local redirection. backend webskd3
    mode http
    server websocks5srv 127.0.0.1:19800
    option http-keep-alive
    timeout server 28s
    timeout tunnel 5h Figure 11: Backend Route Modification to haproxy.conf Attribution GTIG attributes the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-102764 and the subsequent deployment of SAWFLY and BARECLAW to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE (formerly tracked as UNC5221). The tooling and TTPs leveraged within this intrusion align with previously observed activity from ARMORY CASTLE. GTIG has previously reported ARMORY CASTLE exploiting multiple vulnerabilities in edge appliances and deploying an extensive suite of custom tooling to support their objectives, ranging from passive backdoors and webshells to trojanized components of edge devices. ARMORY CASTLE has been active as early as October 2023 and has targeted a wide range of countries and verticals during their operations. Outlook and Implications In past campaigns, ARMORY CASTLE has conducted widespread and opportunistic exploitation following the public disclosure of vulnerabilities it had exploited selectively as zero-days, racing to infiltrate target organizations before patches are deployed. It is possible that we will observe similar widespread exploitation attempts associated with CVE-2026-102764. GTIG assesses with high confidence that ARMORY CASTLE will continue to leverage zero-day vulnerabilities in edge devices to gain access to environments to support their espionage objective. Defenders should also prepare for the possibility that following disclosure of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE may conduct widespread exploitation similar to what GTIG observed in 2024 following the disclosure of CVE-2023-46805 and CVE-2024-21887. Remediation and Hardening Organizations that have not yet applied the BT26-05 patch should immediately assess their exposure and risk, and review additional guidance from BeyondTrust in their blog . CVE-2026-102764 affects all supported Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3 and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to perform file operations on the appliance, which can lead to host-level control and access to every credential the appliance stores or brokers. Any appliance that was reachable from the internet on a vulnerable version during the exploitation window should be treated as potentially compromised until it has been reviewed. Mandiant recommends a phased, patch-first approach that balances containment against disruption to support operations. Immediate Mitigation Organizations should choose among the following options based on their risk tolerance, evidence of compromise, and operational needs. Option 1: Apply the BT26-05 Patch (Mandiant Recommended) Remote Support SaaS : BeyondTrust applied the patch to all SaaS tenants on October 9, 2026. No customer action is required for the appliance itself. The credential and configuration steps in Option 3 still apply. Self-hosted, version 24.3.1 or later : Apply the BT26-05-RS patch from the /appliance interface, or confirm it was applied automatically if the appliance is subscribed to automatic updates. Self-hosted, older than 24.3.1 : Upgrade to a supported version, then apply the patch. Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not remediate prior exposure. If the patch is not visible in /appliance , open a case with BeyondTrust Support referencing BT26-05. Option 2: Isolate Compromised or Suspected Appliances Preserve before acting : Snapshot virtual appliances with memory and export the disk before any change or reboot. For B Series hardware and SaaS tenants, request forensic preservation through BeyondTrust Support. Collect syslog, reverse-proxy or WAF, and perimeter firewall logs for the full exposure window, since an attacker with host access can delete on-appliance logs. Mandiant determined that the actor removed logs throughout the incident. Isolate at the perimeter : Block inbound traffic to the appliance's public address at the firewall rather than in /appliance , so the configuration remains intact for review. Restrict egress : Deny outbound traffic except to BeyondTrust update and licensing endpoints, and log every denied connection. Terminate access paths : End active support sessions and disable new sessions, Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and API accounts from /login . Disable rather than delete so the audit trail survives. Rebuild rather than clean : Redeploy appliances with confirmed or unknown compromise status from a clean, fully patched image. Customers cannot audit the appliance host file system, and host-level persistence survives reboot and configuration reset. Restore only a configuration backup dated before the exposure window, or restore the newest backup while isolated and complete the review in Option 3, Part B, before reconnecting anything. Issue a new TLS certificate and redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the rebuilt appliance. Note : Isolation and session termination interrupt support operations. Organizations should coordinate with help desk and vendor-support stakeholders before proceeding. Option 3: Apply Targeted Compensating Controls The following controls reduce exposure and limit post-exploitation impact. They do not substitute for the patch. Part A: Network Restrictions Restrict access to the /login and /appliance administrative interfaces by IP or network segment at the appliance level. Only representative console, customer portal, and Jump Client traffic should be reachable from the internet. Where operationally possible, place a reverse proxy or WAF with full URI logging in front of the appliance to keep a record of request paths that the appliance cannot alter. Part B: Credential Rotation and Configuration Review Revoke sessions and enrollments : End all active support sessions, then redeploy Jump Clients, Jumpoints, and the representative console from the patched or rebuilt appliance to invalidate existing tokens. Rotate credentials in dependency order : /appliance administrative credentials; /login administrators and local users; API client secrets; security provider bind accounts and SAML signing keys; Remote Support Vault and integrated Password Safe or Privileged Remote Access (PRA) credentials, rotated at the target system; integration credentials (SMTP, syslog, Information Technology Service Management (ITSM) connectors, outbound event secrets); and any credential typed into a support session during the window. Review the /login configuration against a pre-window baseline : user and role changes, particularly Jump Item roles raised to Administrator; group and session policies; API accounts; security providers; Jump Items and Jumpoints; and outbound event or syslog destinations. Remove anything without a change record or a named owner. Review support session reports for the window, including file transfers, to establish which endpoints were accessed and what left them. Every endpoint touched is in scope for downstream hunting. Note : Rotate credentials only after the appliance has been patched or rebuilt. Rotating earlier exposes the new credentials to an attacker who still controls the appliance. Part C: Control Plane Restrictions Require SAML single sign-on with phishing-resistant MFA for all /login users, and remove local accounts except one vaulted break-glass account with alerting on use. Ensure the built-in Admin account is configured with Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) in accordance with the official BeyondTrust Two-Factor Authentication Guidelines . Set the default Jump Item role in every group policy to No Access, and grant roles through policy rather than per user. Scope API accounts to the minimum permission set, with a named automation owner for any account holding user or Jump Item management rights, and rotate API secrets on a schedule. Keep privileged credentials in Password Safe or an external vault with credential injection rather than in the Remote Support Vault, and store only non-interactive service account credentials on the appliance. Apply default-deny outbound filtering from the appliance, allowing only BeyondTrust endpoints and the organization's own syslog and directory servers. Part D: Logging and Detection Engineering Logging and Visibility Forward appliance syslog to a SIEM over TLS with retention that covers a multi-month exposure window, and collect reverse-proxy or WAF and perimeter firewall logs for the appliance's address. Export /login session, team activity, and user audit reports on a schedule. Detection Engineering Account and policy changes : user_changed events that raise a Jump Item or team role; user_added , api_account , and security_provider events with no change ticket; any change to outbound events or syslog destinations. Authentication : /login success from residential-broadband or commercial-VPN address space, and administrative logins outside business hours. Session activity : file-transfer events, and sessions started by accounts whose roles changed during the window. Request paths : at the reverse proxy or WAF, paths outside the known Remote Support path set, including unknown .php paths and WebSocket upgrades from outside support staff and endpoint address ranges. Anti-forensics: gaps in syslog forwarding from the appliance; an interruption bounded by a single session is a strong indicator of log tampering. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users. author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"

    $b32 = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567" ascii wide
    $rc4 = "range(0,255)" ascii wide
    $pack = "pack('H*'," ascii wide
    $eval = "@eval(" ascii wide
    $code404 = "http_response_code(404)" ascii wide

    filesize < 20KB and
    all of them
} rule G_Hunting_Backdoor_BARECLAW_1 {

    author = "Google Threat Intelligence Group"
